nameStory: The American eel gets its name from its snake-like, winding body that resembles the European eel but is found exclusively in American waters. The word 'eel' comes from the Old English 'ǣl,' reflecting how these slippery, elongated fish have fascinated people for centuries with their mysterious migrations across ocean basins.
description: The American eel is a remarkable snake-like fish with an incredibly long, slender body that can grow up to 3-4 feet in length. Its smooth, dark olive to brown coloration and continuous fin running along its back and belly make it unmistakable in New England waters. Despite looking scaleless, it's actually covered in tiny scales hidden beneath a thick layer of slippery mucus that makes it nearly impossible to grip with bare hands.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely long, snake-like body that feels incredibly slippery and muscular when handled, covered in thick mucus that makes it seem scaleless

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single continuous fin runs from mid-back around the tail and along the belly like a ribbon, with small pectoral fins near the head and no pelvic fins at all

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Olive green to brown on top with lighter yellow-green or grayish belly, with eels from clear water appearing lighter than those from dark, tannin-stained streams

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Terminal mouth position with a slightly pointed snout, well-suited for hunting small prey in mud and crevices

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Can reach 3-4 feet in length, with females typically growing much larger than males

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in both freshwater rivers and coastal estuaries, often hiding in mud, sand, or gravel during the day at depths of 5-6 feet

habitat: American eels live in both freshwater rivers and coastal estuaries throughout New England, from the Connecticut River system north to the Saint Lawrence River. During the day, they burrow into soft mud, sand, or gravel bottoms near shore, typically at depths of 5-6 feet. You'll find them in slow-moving rivers, tidal marshes, and brackish waters where they can easily hide among submerged logs, rocks, and vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Young glass eels migrate into freshwater systems, appearing translucent and thread-like as they move upstream. Adult eels become more active as water temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when yellow eels actively hunt at night for crustaceans and aquatic insects, spending days buried in bottom sediments.
seasonality.fall: Mature eels begin their remarkable migration back to the Atlantic Ocean, transforming into silver eels as they prepare for their spawning journey to the Sargasso Sea.
seasonality.winter: Eels become sluggish and bury deeper into mud and sediment, entering a state of reduced activity until spring warming.

funFact: Every single American eel in New England was born in the same place—the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda—and somehow found their way back to our rivers as transparent 'glass eels,' yet scientists still don't know exactly how they navigate thousands of miles to get here.
confusionNotes: American eels are sometimes confused with lampreys, but lampreys have a circular, sucker-like mouth and no paired fins, while eels have normal jaws and small pectoral fins. Remember: eels have jaws that bite, lampreys have sucker mouths that attach.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their snake-like appearance, American eels are true fish with gills and scales, not reptiles. Their incredible sliminess comes from a protective mucus coating that helps them breathe through their skin and squeeze through incredibly tight spaces during their migrations.
compareHints: The American eel is the only species of freshwater eel found in New England waters, making identification straightforward once you recognize the basic eel body plan. While other elongated fish like burbot exist in the region, none share the eel's continuous dorsal and anal fins or extreme slippery texture. The American eel's catadromous lifestyle—living in fresh water but spawning in the ocean—also sets it apart from most other New England fish species.
